To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

AH’s CE strategy for the TCB was successful because it (1) was based on the values of the company, (2) built on existing social networks, (3) facilitated farmer-to-farner engagement, (4) focused engagement on farmer groups, (5) strengthened relationships of trust through experiential learning, and (6) helped farmers to “learn marketing”.

(1) CE can play a key role in the adoption of biotechnologies by small-holder farmers; (2) CE is not a one-size-fits-all approach; rather, it must be tailored to the specific characteristics of the technology, the farmers, and the local context; (3) CE must be designed to be “values-based”; and (4) CE can be designed to help farmers learn how to “play the marketing game” and thereby increase their incomes.

AH’s CE strategy was successful because it: (1) was based on the values of “empowerment” and “collaboration”, (2) focused on building trust and relationships of trust, (3) was based on an empirical, “learning by doing” approach, and (4) focused on helping farmers learn to market the TCB.
In summary, our research is concerned with

how CE can help to create the “social space” in which new agricultural technologies and practices can be successfully introduced, and how this “social space” can be designed and managed to facilitate the uptake of new technologies and practices.
how CE strategies and processes are designed and implemented in order to achieve the desired outcomes.

how CE strategies are developed and deployed in the process of designing and delivering agricultural technologies for global health, and with how CE is related to the adoption of those technologies by farmers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

AH’s CE strategy was effective because it focused on the social, economic and institutional factors affecting the adoption and diffusion of the technology, and on the human relationships and social networks through which these factors were influenced.

CE can be a critical factor in the success or failure of new agricultural biotechnology projects, but the design of CE programs must be based on a deep understanding of the values and interests of the community of farmers and stakeholders involved.

the AH approach was a successful one in that it helped to build a community of farmers that were able to adopt and use the TCB, but it was not successful in that it did not lead to a more widespread uptake of the TBC among small-hold farmers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CE should be understood as a “value-added” process of social learning, rather than as a mere “add-on” to the technology itself.
CE is not just about building trust, it is about helping people to build trust in each other, and in the technologies that they use to improve their lives.

the AH experience demonstrates that CE is not only an important component of the design process for new technologies, but also that CE can play a key role in shaping the nature of the technology itself.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the design of CE strategies should be informed not only by the technical requirements of the technology in question, but also by the “values” of the stakeholders involved in the CE process.
CE is not simply a means to an end, but rather an end in itself, and that the values of those involved in CE are critical to the success or failure of a CE strategy.
CE is not simply an optional extra, or something that is added on to the design of a new technology or innovation.
